title: ATD 2026: Hallway chats, cheaper failures and bending systems
author: Jit Gosai
text: I’ve been at Agile Testing Days (ATD) for the last four days, and what a ride! They pretty much take over the hotel in Potsdam, Germany, with speakers, attendees and organisers all packed into the venue. From around 8am till 11pm, there’s something going on. Yoga, breakfast, Lean Coffee, games, hallway conversations, panel discussions, and that’s before you even get into the talks and workshops. Hallway chats I spent a lot of time diving in and out of talks and chatting with folks. Honestly, these are some of the best parts of conferences. If you’ve got something bouncing around your head and want to get other people’s opinions, this is where to do it. Now I’m pretty lucky. Having spoken at conferences over the years, I’ve made friends with lots of people, so sitting down to pick their brains is much easier for me. But I’d still encourage you to speak to the speakers. If they’re hanging around the public spaces, chances are they’re happy to chat. Just smile, introduce yourself and dive in. If you saw their talk, share something you liked or, even better, something you took away from it. Trust me , they’ll love that! I spent a lot of time simply asking, “Hey, would you be up for a chat? I’d love to get your take on something.” Another great question was “Who else should I speak to?” Often they’d suggest someone else, and if I didn’t know them, I’d ask for an introduction. Before you know it, you’re slowly building out your network. A few ATD 2026 takeaways So what am I taking away from ATD this year? Here are four ideas that are still bouncing around my head. Making failure cheap - Clare Norman I shared a little of Clare’s opening keynote on Notes , but something really connected with my learning from failure series. How do we make failure cheaper so we can learn from it rather than just trying to prevent it? But Clare helped me see something I’d not really considered. A failure doesn’t cost everyone the same. Think about a reminder feature. Forgetting to take out your bins isn’t the end of the world, but missing a reminder to take your medication could have much more serious consequences. So when we’re making failure cheap, we need to think about who is actually paying the cost. If you watch any talk from ATD, then I’d highly recommend this one . So many of Clare’s ideas connect to quality engineering. Levers, signals and noise - Elisabeth Hendrickson and Joel Tosi I loved this framing. Levers are things within a system we can influence or change, while signals are observable changes that tell us something meaningful is happening. I often shortcut signals to feedback, but I like this framing better. It makes me think more carefully about what we’re observing and whether it’s actually telling us anything useful. This connected closely with my talk on sociotechnical systems. If we want to change how our systems behave, we need to understand which levers we can pull and what signals might tell us whether we’re making a difference. And, importantly, how do we distinguish those signals from noise? Elisabeth and Joel have also written a book on this, Signals & Levers , which is going on my reading list! Bend the system - Anne-Marie Charrett Anne-Marie gave me such a simple idea that had never really occurred to me before. We’re regularly told we need to change the system. I’ve probably said it countless times myself. But what if changing the system isn’t possible, at least not right now? Why not try bending it instead? Shift the language, tweak a default approach, build on existing momentum or make the right things the easy things. Small nudges might not give us the change we’re looking for immediately, but they could start moving things in the right direction. I really like this idea, especially when thinking about long-term culture change. Anne-Marie also has a new book out - The Quality Coach’s Handbook .
